notes.meaning: The people and leaders in Jerusalem failed to recognize who Jesus was. When they condemned Him to die, they actually fulfilled the words of the prophets that were read in their synagogues every Sabbath. Their ignorance did not excuse their sin, but God used their wicked choices to carry out His divine plan.

The leaders could find no real crime that deserved the death penalty. Even so, they demanded that the Roman governor Pilate have Jesus put to death. This showed the complete innocence of Jesus and the deep injustice of His execution.

After everything the Scriptures foretold about His suffering had been fulfilled, Jesus was taken down from the cross and laid in a tomb. Being buried confirmed that He was truly dead and completely separated from earthly life. His enemies thought they had shut Him away forever.

Death could not hold Jesus, because God raised Him from the dead. While humans did their worst to destroy Him, God reversed their action with almighty power. This miracle proved that Jesus was innocent and that His mission was approved by God.

Jesus appeared alive over many days to the followers who had traveled with Him from Galilee to Jerusalem. These disciples knew Him well and could not have been easily fooled. They became bold eyewitnesses, sharing the truth of His resurrection with their fellow Jews.

Paul and Barnabas proclaimed the gospel, which is the good news that God keeps His word. The ancient promises made to the fathers of Israel were now arriving in real history. The coming of the Savior was the best news any sinner could receive.

God fulfilled His promises to Israel by raising up Jesus from the dead. By quoting Psalm 2, Paul showed that the resurrection openly demonstrated that Jesus is God's royal Son. The day of His rising brought His divine identity and kingship out into full public view.

When God raised Jesus from the dead, He raised Him never to die or rot in the grave again. Unlike others who were brought back to life only to die later, Jesus lives forever. This fulfilled God's promise to David of an eternal King and trustworthy blessings.

Paul cites another psalm where David says God will not allow His Holy One to experience decay. This Scripture promised that the Messiah's physical body would never rot in a grave. It guaranteed that He would rise before corruption could touch Him.

King David faithfully served God's purpose for the people of his own time, and then he died. His body was buried with his ancestors and turned to dust. Because David rotted in the grave, the promise in the psalm could not have been written about him.

In contrast to David, Jesus was raised up by God on the third day and never decayed. This proves that David's prophetic song applied directly to Jesus and no one else. Christ alone is the living King whose body saw no corruption.

Paul urged his hearers to understand that through Jesus alone, full forgiveness of sins is offered to them. Forgiveness means that God cancels the debt of our sins through Christ's sacrifice. This is the great blessing that restores sinners to peace with God.

Everyone who believes in Jesus is justified, which means they are declared completely righteous and cleared of all guilt before God. The old ceremonies and animal sacrifices in the law of Moses could never wash away sin or clear the human conscience. What the law could never do, Christ accomplished fully on the cross.

Paul gave a serious warning to make sure his listeners did not bring ancient prophetic curses upon themselves. Spiritual privilege gives no safety to those who remain stubborn in unbelief. God gives warnings so people will wake up and turn to Him before judgment falls.

Quoting the prophet Habakkuk, Paul warned that those who mock God's message will be stunned by His judgment and perish. In the past, the people refused to believe that God would bring destruction through the Babylonians, but it happened anyway. Rejecting the gospel of Christ brings the same certain ruin.

As the meeting in the synagogue came to a close, people urged Paul and Barnabas to preach the same message again on the next Sabbath. Those who listened were deeply impressed by what they had heard and wanted to learn more. True hunger for the word of God always seeks to hear it again.

After the crowd was dismissed, many Jews and Gentile converts to Judaism followed the apostles to hear more. Paul and Barnabas spoke warmly with them and urged them to remain steadfast in the grace of God. Holding to this grace meant continuing to rely entirely on Christ for salvation.

On the next Sabbath day, nearly the entire city came out to hear the preaching of God's word. News about the apostles' message had spread widely during the week through private conversations. A massive crowd of both Jews and Gentiles showed up eager to listen.

When the Jewish leaders saw the huge crowds, they were filled with bitter jealousy. They did not want the Gentiles treated as equals, and they resented the apostles' popularity. Because they could not answer the apostles with truth, they began interrupting, arguing, and speaking evil against Jesus.

Paul and Barnabas were not intimidated and spoke out with holy courage. They explained that God's word had to be preached to the Jews first because they were the covenant people. But since the leaders pushed the message away, they condemned themselves as unfit for eternal life, and the apostles turned to the Gentiles.

The apostles explained that preaching to the Gentiles was an obedience to God's command found in the prophet Isaiah. The Lord promised that the Messiah would be a light to other nations and bring salvation to the farthest parts of the earth. In taking the gospel to the non-Jews, the apostles were carrying out that ancient divine purpose.

When the Gentiles heard that God's offer of salvation included them, they rejoiced and honored the message of the Lord. Those who were appointed for eternal life believed in Christ and embraced the gospel. Saving faith took root as God worked in their hearts.

differ.view: God chose specific individuals for eternal life before the world began, and His sovereign choice is what causes them to believe.
The word describes God's present grace awakening faith in the hearts of those who did not push the gospel away, rather than an eternal decree choosing only some.

notes.meaning: The good news of the Lord did not stay inside the city but spread quickly across the whole surrounding territory. The new believers were so changed by the message that they shared it everywhere they went. The truth shone outward like the rising sun.

The opposing leaders influenced prominent Gentile women who worshipped at the synagogue, along with the city rulers. By spreading false charges, they stirred up an angry backlash against Paul and Barnabas. The authorities then drove the two preachers out of their region by force.

Before departing, Paul and Barnabas shook the dust off their feet as a solemn warning against the city's rejection, just as Jesus had instructed. This action showed that the apostles were free from guilt and that the opposers were spiritually defiled by their unbelief. The two missionaries then traveled on to the city of Iconium.

Even though their teachers had been driven away and trouble surrounded them, the new disciples were filled with joy and the Holy Spirit. Earthly persecution could not steal the peace and confidence that came from knowing Christ. The Holy Spirit gave them courage to stand firm through every trial.
